title: Ball Rebounding from a Wall
topic: Mathematical Routines · Impulse from a time-dependent force

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 1 (Mathematical Routines)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: A ball of mass m moves right with speed v0 toward a rigid wall on the right side of a horizontal surface

Part A (i), Figure 2: Blank axes of force magnitude F versus time t, with dashed vertical lines at tc/2 and tc

prompt: A ball of mass \(m\) moves to the right with speed \(v_0\) on a horizontal frictionless surface and strikes a rigid wall. The ball is in contact with the wall from \(t = 0\) to \(t = t_c\) and rebounds to the left with speed \(\tfrac{1}{2}v_0\). During the contact, the magnitude of the force exerted by the wall on the ball is modeled as \(F(t) = F_{\max}\left[1 - \left(\dfrac{2t}{t_c} - 1\right)^2\right]\), where \(F_{\max}\) is a constant.

parts.label: A (i)
parts.text: On axes of force magnitude versus time, sketch \(F(t)\) from \(t = 0\) to \(t = t_c\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches a curve that is zero at \(t = 0\) and \(t = t_c\) and positive in between.
commonErrors: draws a nonzero force at the endpoints
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A curve starting and ending on the time axis.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches a symmetric, concave-down curve with its maximum value \(F_{\max}\) at \(t = \tfrac{t_c}{2}\).
commonErrors: places the maximum at an endpoint
draws a triangle with straight sides
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A downward parabola peaking at Fmax at tc/2.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 200" width="340" height="200" role="img" aria-label="Blank axes of force magnitude F versus time t, with dashed vertical lines at tc/2 and tc" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="40" y1="170" x2="311" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><polygon points="320,170 311,174 311,166" fill="currentColor" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="40" y1="180" x2="40" y2="29" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><polygon points="40,20 44,29 36,29" fill="currentColor" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="30" y="26" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">F</text><text x="325" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">t</text><text x="32" y="184" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">O</text><line x1="150" y1="30" x2="150" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="150" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">t꜀/2</text><line x1="260" y1="30" x2="260" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="260" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">t꜀</text></svg>
figures.alt: Blank axes of force magnitude F versus time t, with dashed vertical lines at tc/2 and tc
figures.caption: Figure 2

parts.label: A (ii)
parts.text: Derive an expression for \(F_{\max}\) in terms of \(m\), \(v_0\), \(t_c\), and physical constants, as appropriate. Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the impulse-momentum theorem as an integral, \(J = \int F\,dt = \Delta p\).
commonErrors: uses J = FΔt with a constant force
starts with F = ma and a constant acceleration

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the magnitude of the change in momentum as \(m\left(v_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}v_0\right) = \tfrac{3}{2}mv_0\).
Correctly evaluates the integral, \(\int_0^{t_c}F_{\max}\left[1 - \left(\tfrac{2t}{t_c} - 1\right)^2\right]dt = \tfrac{2}{3}F_{\max}t_c\).
Arrives at \(F_{\max} = \dfrac{9mv_0}{4t_c}\) (or an answer consistent with earlier work).

parts.label: B (i)
parts.text: Derive an expression for the work done by the wall on the ball during the collision in terms of \(m\), \(v_0\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses the work-energy theorem, \(W = \Delta K\).
commonErrors: computes work as force times the contact time

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(K_i = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2\) and \(K_f = \tfrac{1}{2}m\left(\tfrac{v_0}{2}\right)^2\).
Arrives at \(W = -\tfrac{3}{8}mv_0^2\), including the negative sign.

parts.label: B (ii)
parts.text: Indicate whether the collision is elastic or inelastic. Briefly justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates inelastic, justified by the loss of kinetic energy (the negative work in part B (i)) or the rebound speed being less than the incoming speed.
commonErrors: calls it elastic because the ball bounces back
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Inelastic, because the ball leaves with less kinetic energy than it arrived with.

sampleResponse: A (i) A symmetric downward parabola from 0 at \(t = 0\) to \(F_{\max}\) at \(t_c/2\) and back to 0 at \(t_c\). (ii) \(\int_0^{t_c}F\,dt = \Delta p\). The momentum changes from \(mv_0\) to the right to \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv_0\) to the left, so \(|\Delta p| = \tfrac{3}{2}mv_0\). With \(u = \tfrac{2t}{t_c} - 1\), \(\int_0^{t_c}F\,dt = F_{\max}\tfrac{t_c}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}(1 - u^2)\,du = \tfrac{2}{3}F_{\max}t_c\). So \(F_{\max} = \dfrac{9mv_0}{4t_c}\). B (i) \(W = \Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}m\left(\tfrac{v_0}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = -\tfrac{3}{8}mv_0^2\). (ii) Inelastic: the ball loses kinetic energy.

title: Oscillator with a Stiff Bumper
topic: Translation Between Representations · Piecewise simple harmonic motion

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 2 (Translation Between Representations)

stimulus.content: Figure 1: A block on a frictionless surface is attached to a spring of constant k from the left wall. A shorter bumper spring of constant 3k, also fixed to the left wall, has its free end at x = 0, just touching the block when the main spring is relaxed

prompt: A block of mass \(m\) on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring of spring constant \(k\) whose other end is fixed to a wall. The block's position is \(x\), with \(x = 0\) where the spring is relaxed. A second, massless spring of spring constant \(3k\) is fixed to the left wall so that its free end is exactly at \(x = 0\); the block pushes on it only when \(x < 0\) and does not stick to it. The block is released from rest at \(x = +A\).

figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: On axes of the \(x\)-component of the net force on the block versus \(x\), sketch \(F_x\) for \(-\tfrac{A}{2} \le x \le A\).

rubricPoints.criterion: For \(x > 0\), draws a straight line through the origin with negative slope (magnitude \(k\)), reaching \(-kA\) at \(x = A\).
commonErrors: draws a positive force for x > 0
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A straight line from the origin down to −kA at x = A.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A straight line rising to +kA at x = A.

rubricPoints.criterion: For \(x < 0\), draws a straight line through the origin with a negative slope four times as steep (magnitude \(4k\)), continuous at \(x = 0\).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A steeper straight line rising to +2kA at x = −A/2.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The same slope on both sides.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Derive an expression for the position of the block when it first momentarily comes to rest on the left side of \(x = 0\), in terms of \(A\). Begin with a fundamental physics principle.

rubricPoints.criterion: Begins with conservation of mechanical energy for the block-spring system.
Writes the initial energy as \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\).
commonErrors: includes the 3k spring in the initial energy

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the final energy as the sum of both springs' energies, \(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(3k)x^2 = 2kx^2\).
Arrives at \(x = -\tfrac{A}{2}\) (a distance \(\tfrac{A}{2}\) left of \(x = 0\)).

parts.label: C
parts.text: On axes of \(x\) versus \(t\), sketch the block's position for one full cycle starting at \(t = 0\), when the block is released.

rubricPoints.criterion: Starts at \(x = +A\) with zero slope and draws smooth sinusoidal segments.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Starts at the top with a horizontal tangent.

rubricPoints.criterion: Shows the minimum position as \(-\tfrac{A}{2}\), smaller in magnitude than the maximum.
commonErrors: draws a symmetric oscillation between +A and −A
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The graph is symmetric about the t-axis.

rubricPoints.criterion: Shows the block spending less time on the negative side than on the positive side of each cycle (half as long).
commonErrors: draws equal times on both sides
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The negative lobe is narrower than the positive lobe.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Derive an expression for the period of the motion in terms of \(m\), \(k\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the time for \(x > 0\) as half a period of an oscillator with spring constant \(k\): \(\pi\sqrt{m/k}\).
commonErrors: uses the full period for one side

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the time for \(x < 0\) as half a period with effective spring constant \(4k\): \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{m/k}\).
commonErrors: uses 3k as the effective spring constant

rubricPoints.criterion: Adds the two times to get \(T = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}\).

sampleResponse: A For \(x > 0\), \(F_x = -kx\): a line from the origin to \(-kA\) at \(x = A\). For \(x < 0\), \(F_x = -4kx\): a line four times as steep, reaching \(+2kA\) at \(x = -A/2\). B \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(3k)x^2 = 2kx^2\), so \(x = -\tfrac{A}{2}\). C A cosine-like curve from \(+A\), down through 0 into a narrower dip to \(-A/2\), and back to \(+A\). D The positive side takes half a period with \(k\): \(\pi\sqrt{m/k}\). The negative side takes half a period with \(4k\): \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{m/k}\). So \(T = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}\).

title: Rotational Inertia of a Flywheel
topic: Experimental Design and Analysis · Rotational dynamics and linearization

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 3 (Experimental Design and Analysis)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: A large flywheel on an axle of radius r. A string wraps around the axle, runs horizontally over a pulley at the table edge, and holds a hanging mass m

Part C, Table 1
Hanging mass m (kg) | Acceleration a (m/s²)
0.050 | 1.95
0.100 | 3.30
0.150 | 4.15
0.200 | 4.90
0.250 | 5.50

prompt: A flywheel is mounted on a frictionless horizontal axle. A light string is wrapped around the axle, which has radius \(r = 0.050\text{ m}\), passes over a light frictionless pulley, and is attached to a hanging object of mass \(m\), as shown in Figure 1. Students want to determine the rotational inertia \(I\) of the flywheel and axle. They have a set of hanging masses, a meterstick, a stopwatch, and a motion sensor.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="360" height="200" role="img" aria-label="A large flywheel on an axle of radius r. A string wraps around the axle, runs horizontally over a pulley at the table edge, and holds a hanging mass m" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="90" cy="80" r="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><circle cx="90" cy="80" r="12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="90" cy="80" r="3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="90" y1="68" x2="290" y2="68" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="290" cy="80" r="12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="302" y1="80" x2="302" y2="150" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><rect x="287" y="150" width="30" height="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="302" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">m</text><line x1="90" y1="80" x2="102" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="100" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">r</text><text x="90" y="160" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">flywheel</text><text x="255" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">pulley</text></svg>
figures.alt: A large flywheel on an axle of radius r. A string wraps around the axle, runs horizontally over a pulley at the table edge, and holds a hanging mass m
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe an experimental procedure for collecting data that could be graphed to determine \(I\). Include enough detail that another student could replicate it, and a method to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes measuring the acceleration of the hanging object (with the motion sensor, or by timing a fall from rest over a measured distance, a = 2h/t²) for several different hanging masses.
commonErrors: varies the radius instead of the mass
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: For five masses, release from rest and use the motion sensor to find the acceleration from the slope of the v–t graph.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Drop the mass and time it.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a valid way to reduce uncertainty, such as repeating trials for each mass and averaging, or using a large fall distance.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Repeat each mass three times and average the accelerations.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Starting with Newton's second law for the hanging object and for the flywheel, show that \(\dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{1}{g} + \dfrac{I}{gr^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{m}\), where \(a\) is the magnitude of the hanging object's acceleration.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(mg - F_T = ma\) for the hanging object and \(F_Tr = I\alpha\) with \(\alpha = a/r\) for the flywheel.
commonErrors: sets the tension equal to mg
omits the rolling constraint a = αr

rubricPoints.criterion: Combines them to \(mg = a\left(m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right)\) and divides by \(mga\) to reach the given expression.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: States the expression without combining the equations.

parts.label: C
parts.text: The students' data are shown in Table 1. (i) Indicate quantities to graph on the vertical and horizontal axes to produce a linear graph. (ii) Plot the data, including any calculated values, on a graph with labeled axes, units, and a linear scale. (iii) Draw a best-fit line.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates \(1/a\) versus \(1/m\) (or an equivalent linearization such as \(m/a\) versus \(m\)).
Labels both axes with quantities and correct units, using linear scales.

rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Five correctly calculated and plotted points.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws a straight best-fit line consistent with the trend of the data.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: One straight line near all points.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Hanging mass m (kg) 0.050, Acceleration a (m/s²) 1.95; Hanging mass m (kg) 0.100, Acceleration a (m/s²) 3.30; Hanging mass m (kg) 0.150, Acceleration a (m/s²) 4.15; Hanging mass m (kg) 0.200, Acceleration a (m/s²) 4.90; Hanging mass m (kg) 0.250, Acceleration a (m/s²) 5.50

parts.label: D
parts.text: Using your best-fit line, calculate an experimental value for \(I\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses the slope of the best-fit line and relates it to \(I\): slope \(= \dfrac{I}{gr^2}\).
commonErrors: uses the intercept to find I
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: I = m r² from one row of the table.

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \(I\) between about \(4.5\times10^{-4}\) and \(5.5\times10^{-4}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

sampleResponse: A Hang a mass, measure it with a balance, release it from rest, and use the motion sensor to record its velocity; the slope of the velocity-time graph is \(a\). Repeat three times for each of five masses and average. B For the hanging object, \(mg - F_T = ma\). For the flywheel, \(F_Tr = I\alpha = Ia/r\), so \(F_T = Ia/r^2\). Then \(mg = a(m + I/r^2)\), and dividing by \(mga\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{1}{g} + \dfrac{I}{gr^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{m}\). C Graph \(1/a\) versus \(1/m\): points (20, 0.513), (10, 0.303), (6.67, 0.241), (5.0, 0.204), (4.0, 0.182) with a straight best-fit line. D Slope \(\approx 0.0207\), so \(I = (\text{slope})gr^2 \approx 0.0207 \times 9.8 \times 0.0025 \approx 5.1\times10^{-4}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

title: Hoop and Cylinder Race

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 4 (Qualitative/Quantitative Translation)

stimulus.content: Figure 1: A hoop and a solid cylinder side by side at the top of an incline of angle theta

prompt: A thin hoop and a uniform solid cylinder have the same mass \(M\) and radius \(R\). The rotational inertia of the hoop about its center is \(MR^2\), and that of the cylinder is \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\). Both are released from rest at the same time from the top of an incline that makes an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, and both roll without slipping.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 170" width="360" height="170" role="img" aria-label="A hoop and a solid cylinder side by side at the top of an incline of angle theta" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="20,150 340,150 20,30" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><circle cx="70" cy="23" r="16" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="110" cy="38" r="16" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><text x="285" y="142" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">θ</text><text x="70" y="6" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">hoop</text><text x="150" y="30" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">cylinder</text></svg>
figures.alt: A hoop and a solid cylinder side by side at the top of an incline of angle theta
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Indicate which object reaches the bottom of the incline first, or whether they arrive at the same time. Justify your answer using qualitative reasoning beyond referencing equations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that the solid cylinder reaches the bottom first.
commonErrors: indicates the same time because the masses are equal

rubricPoints.criterion: States that both objects convert the same amount of gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy (or experience the same gravitational force along the incline).
commonErrors: claims the hoop has more potential energy
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Both lose the same gravitational potential energy over the same height.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that the hoop has more mass far from its axis (greater rotational inertia), so a larger share of its kinetic energy goes into rotation, leaving less translational speed at each point.
commonErrors: says the hoop has more friction
mentions rotational inertia without linking it to speed
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: More of the hoop’s energy goes into spinning, so it moves down the incline more slowly.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The hoop has a larger rotational inertia.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Starting with Newton's second law in translational and rotational form, derive an expression for the acceleration of the center of an object of mass \(M\), radius \(R\), and rotational inertia \(\beta MR^2\) rolling without slipping down the incline. Express your answer in terms of \(\beta\), \(\theta\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma\) and \(fR = I\alpha\).
Uses the rolling condition \(a = \alpha R\) to get \(f = \beta Ma\).
Arrives at \(a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \beta}\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: Indicate whether your expression from part B is or is not consistent with your answer in part A. Justify by referencing the expression.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses functional dependence language: the acceleration decreases as \(\beta\) increases.
commonErrors: restates part A without referencing the expression

rubricPoints.criterion: Applies \(\beta = 1\) for the hoop and \(\beta = \tfrac{1}{2}\) for the cylinder to conclude the cylinder accelerates faster, consistent with part A.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Hoop: \(a = \tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta\); cylinder: \(a = \tfrac{2}{3}g\sin\theta\); the cylinder wins, consistent with part A.

sampleResponse: A The cylinder arrives first. Both lose the same gravitational potential energy as they descend. The hoop's mass is all at the rim, so it has the larger rotational inertia and more of its kinetic energy goes into rotation, leaving it with a smaller translational speed at every point. B \(Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma\) and \(fR = \beta MR^2\alpha\) with \(\alpha = a/R\), so \(f = \beta Ma\) and \(a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \beta}\). C Consistent: a larger \(\beta\) gives a smaller acceleration. The hoop (\(\beta = 1\)) has \(a = \tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta\) and the cylinder (\(\beta = \tfrac{1}{2}\)) has \(a = \tfrac{2}{3}g\sin\theta\).

title: Coasting Boat with Water Drag
topic: Mathematical Routines · Resistive force proportional to velocity

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 1 (Mathematical Routines)

stimulus.content: Figure 1: A boat of mass M moves to the right with speed v0 on water; the drag force on it points left

prompt: A boat of mass \(M\) is moving in a straight line with speed \(v_0\) at time \(t = 0\), when its engine is shut off. The only horizontal force on the boat afterward is a resistive force from the water, \(\vec{F} = -b\vec{v}\), where \(b\) is a positive constant.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 100" width="360" height="100" role="img" aria-label="A boat of mass M moves to the right with speed v0 on water; the drag force on it points left" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M60 50 L240 50 L215 80 L85 80 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><rect x="120" y="28" width="50" height="22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><path d="M10 82 Q30 76 50 82 T90 82 T130 82 T170 82 T210 82 T250 82 T290 82 T330 82 T350 82" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="250" y1="50" x2="301" y2="50" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.4"/><polygon points="310,50 301,54 301,46" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1"/><text x="285" y="42" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">v₀</text><line x1="60" y1="65" x2="27" y2="65" stroke="#ec4899" stroke-width="2.4"/><polygon points="18,65 27,61 27,69" fill="#ec4899" stroke="#ec4899" stroke-width="1"/><text x="30" y="58" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">F</text></svg>
figures.alt: A boat of mass M moves to the right with speed v0 on water; the drag force on it points left
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A (i)
parts.text: On axes of speed versus time, sketch the speed of the boat for \(t \ge 0\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches a curve starting at \(v_0\) that decreases and is concave up.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A decaying curve starting at v0, steep at first then flattening.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A straight line from v0 to zero.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches the curve approaching zero asymptotically, never crossing or touching the time axis.
commonErrors: shows the speed reaching zero at a finite time
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The curve levels toward the axis without reaching it.

parts.label: A (ii)
parts.text: Derive an expression for the speed \(v(t)\) of the boat as a function of time in terms of \(M\), \(b\), \(v_0\), \(t\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes Newton's second law as a differential equation, \(M\dfrac{dv}{dt} = -bv\).
Separates variables, \(\dfrac{dv}{v} = -\dfrac{b}{M}dt\).
commonErrors: separates incorrectly, leaving v on both sides
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: \(dv = -\dfrac{b}{M}v\,dt\) integrated as if v were constant.

rubricPoints.criterion: Integrates with correct limits, \(\int_{v_0}^{v}\dfrac{dv'}{v'} = -\dfrac{b}{M}\int_0^t dt'\), giving \(\ln\dfrac{v}{v_0} = -\dfrac{bt}{M}\).
commonErrors: omits the limits or constant of integration

rubricPoints.criterion: Arrives at \(v(t) = v_0e^{-bt/M}\).

parts.label: B
parts.text: Derive an expression for the total distance the boat travels after the engine is shut off, in terms of \(M\), \(b\), \(v_0\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Integrates the velocity from \(t = 0\) to \(t \to \infty\), \(x = \int_0^\infty v_0e^{-bt/M}\,dt\) (or uses \(M\,v\,\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -bv\)).
commonErrors: multiplies v0 by a stopping time

rubricPoints.criterion: Arrives at \(x = \dfrac{Mv_0}{b}\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: A second boat of mass \(2M\) with the same \(b\) and the same initial speed \(v_0\) shuts off its engine. Indicate whether the second boat's total coasting distance is greater than, less than, or equal to twice the first boat's distance. Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that it is equal to twice the first boat’s distance.
Justifies with the linear dependence \(x \propto M\) from part B, or by reasoning that the same force at each speed produces half the deceleration of the heavier boat.
commonErrors: claims that more mass means more drag

sampleResponse: A (i) A concave-up curve decreasing from \(v_0\) and approaching zero asymptotically. (ii) \(M\dfrac{dv}{dt} = -bv\), so \(\dfrac{dv}{v} = -\dfrac{b}{M}dt\). Integrating from \(v_0\) at \(t = 0\): \(\ln\dfrac{v}{v_0} = -\dfrac{bt}{M}\), so \(v = v_0e^{-bt/M}\). B \(x = \int_0^\infty v_0e^{-bt/M}dt = \dfrac{Mv_0}{b}\). C Equal to twice: \(x \propto M\), so doubling the mass doubles the coasting distance.

title: Ball Launched from a Moving Cart
topic: Translation Between Representations · Momentum conservation and projectile motion

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 2 (Translation Between Representations)

stimulus.content: Figure 1: A cart of mass 3M with a vertical launcher tube holding a ball of mass M moves right with speed v0 on a level track

prompt: A cart of mass \(3M\) carries a spring launcher loaded with a ball of mass \(M\). The cart and ball move together to the right with speed \(v_0\) on a level frictionless track. At \(t = 0\) the launcher fires the ball straight up relative to the cart with speed \(u\). Air resistance is negligible.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 140" width="380" height="140" role="img" aria-label="A cart of mass 3M with a vertical launcher tube holding a ball of mass M moves right with speed v0 on a level track" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="10" y1="118" x2="370" y2="118" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="110" y="75" width="120" height="34" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="170" y="98" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">3M</text><circle cx="135" cy="113" r="6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="205" cy="113" r="6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><rect x="160" y="35" width="20" height="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><circle cx="170" cy="28" r="8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><text x="186" y="24" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">M</text><line x1="240" y1="92" x2="291" y2="92" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.4"/><polygon points="300,92 291,96 291,88" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1"/><text x="270" y="84" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">v₀</text></svg>
figures.alt: A cart of mass 3M with a vertical launcher tube holding a ball of mass M moves right with speed v0 on a level track
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Before launch, the horizontal momentum of the cart-ball system is represented by an arrow 4 grid units long pointing to the right. Draw arrows on the same scale to represent the horizontal component of the momentum of the cart and of the ball immediately after the launch.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws the cart’s horizontal momentum as a rightward arrow 3 units long.
commonErrors: shrinks the cart’s arrow because the ball was pushed

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws the ball’s horizontal momentum as a rightward arrow 1 unit long.
commonErrors: draws zero horizontal momentum for the ball

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws arrows whose total is 4 units, showing the system’s horizontal momentum is unchanged because the launch force is vertical.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Derive an expression for the horizontal distance the ball travels from launch until it returns to its launch height, in terms of \(u\), \(v_0\), and physical constants, as appropriate. Then indicate where the ball lands relative to the launcher.

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds the time of flight from vertical motion, \(t = \dfrac{2u}{g}\).
commonErrors: uses u/g, the time to the top

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses the ball's constant horizontal velocity \(v_0\) to get \(x = \dfrac{2uv_0}{g}\).
commonErrors: uses a horizontal velocity other than v0

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the ball lands back in the launcher because the cart keeps the same horizontal velocity v0 and so travels the same horizontal distance.
commonErrors: says the ball lands behind the cart
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The cart also moves at v0, so it travels the same distance and catches the ball.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The ball lands behind the cart because the cart moves forward.

parts.label: C
parts.text: On separate axes, sketch (i) the vertical velocity component of the ball and (ii) the horizontal velocity component of the cart, each from just after launch until the ball returns to launch height at \(t_f\). Take up and right as positive.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches the ball's vertical velocity as a straight line starting at \(+u\) with slope \(-g\).
Shows the vertical velocity crossing zero at \(t_f/2\) and ending at \(-u\) at \(t_f\).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Crosses zero halfway and ends at −u.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches the cart's horizontal velocity as a horizontal line at \(v_0\).
commonErrors: shows the cart speeding up or slowing down
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A line that rises after launch.

parts.label: D
parts.text: The experiment is repeated, but this time the launcher is turned so that it fires the ball horizontally backward (to the left) with speed \(u\) relative to the cart after the launch. Derive an expression for the cart's speed after launch in terms of \(v_0\) and \(u\), and indicate whether the cart speeds up or slows down.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes horizontal momentum conservation using the ball's velocity relative to the ground, \(4Mv_0 = 3Mv_c + M(v_c - u)\).
commonErrors: uses −u as the ball’s ground velocity
uses the velocity relative to the cart before launch

rubricPoints.criterion: Arrives at \(v_c = v_0 + \tfrac{u}{4}\).
Indicates that the cart speeds up, consistent with the launcher pushing the cart forward as it pushes the ball backward.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: It speeds up: the ball pushes back on the launcher in the forward direction.

sampleResponse: A Cart: 3 units to the right; ball: 1 unit to the right. The launch force is vertical, so the total stays 4 units. B Vertically, \(0 = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2\), so \(t = 2u/g\). Horizontally the ball keeps \(v_0\), so \(x = \dfrac{2uv_0}{g}\). The cart also moves at \(v_0\), so the ball lands back in the launcher. C (i) A straight line from \(+u\) with slope \(-g\), crossing zero at \(t_f/2\) and ending at \(-u\). (ii) A horizontal line at \(v_0\). D \(4Mv_0 = 3Mv_c + M(v_c - u)\), so \(v_c = v_0 + \tfrac{u}{4}\): the cart speeds up.

title: Physical Pendulum and the Parallel-Axis Theorem

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 3 (Experimental Design and Analysis)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: A vertical bar hangs from a pivot through one of a row of holes; the pivot is a distance d above the bar’s center of mass

Part C, Table 1
Pivot distance d (m) | Period T (s)
0.05 | 0.92
0.10 | 0.85
0.15 | 0.91
0.20 | 0.98

prompt: A rigid bar of mass \(m = 0.50\text{ kg}\) has holes drilled along its length so it can hang from a frictionless pivot at several distances \(d\) from its center of mass. For small oscillations, the period of a physical pendulum is \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}\), where \(I\) is the rotational inertia about the pivot. Students want to determine the rotational inertia \(I_{cm}\) of the bar about its center of mass.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 240 220" width="240" height="220" role="img" aria-label="A vertical bar hangs from a pivot through one of a row of holes; the pivot is a distance d above the bar’s center of mass" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="105" y="20" width="30" height="190" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><circle cx="120" cy="40" r="3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="120" cy="60" r="3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="120" cy="80" r="3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="120" cy="100" r="3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="120" cy="120" r="3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="120" cy="40" r="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="120" cy="115" r="4" stroke="#ec4899" stroke-width="1.8" fill="#ec4899"/><text x="150" y="119" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">center of mass</text><line x1="90" y1="40" x2="90" y2="115" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="80" y="82" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">d</text><text x="150" y="44" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">pivot</text></svg>
figures.alt: A vertical bar hangs from a pivot through one of a row of holes; the pivot is a distance d above the bar’s center of mass
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe a procedure the students could use to collect data that would allow them to determine I_cm, including a method to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes hanging the bar from several pivot holes, measuring each distance \(d\) with a meterstick, and measuring the period for small-angle oscillations.
commonErrors: varies the mass instead of d
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: For five holes, measure d, displace the bar a few degrees, and time the oscillations.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Swing the bar from one hole and time it.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes timing many oscillations and dividing, or repeating trials and averaging, to reduce uncertainty.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Time 20 oscillations and divide by 20, three times per hole.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Using the parallel-axis theorem, \(I = I_{cm} + md^2\), show that \(T^2d = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}d^2 + \dfrac{4\pi^2I_{cm}}{mg}\), and describe how \(I_{cm}\) can be found from a graph of \(T^2d\) versus \(d^2\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Substitutes the parallel-axis theorem into the period, squares, and multiplies by \(d\) to reach the given expression.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: States the expression without a derivation.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the vertical intercept as \(\dfrac{4\pi^2I_{cm}}{mg}\), so \(I_{cm} = \dfrac{(\text{intercept})mg}{4\pi^2}\).
commonErrors: uses the slope to find I_cm

parts.label: C
parts.text: The students' data are shown in Table 1. (i) Calculate \(d^2\) and \(T^2d\) for each trial. (ii) Plot \(T^2d\) versus \(d^2\) with labeled axes, units, and linear scales. (iii) Draw a best-fit line.

rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Calculated columns that match the data.

rubricPoints.criterion: Labels both axes with quantities and correct units and uses linear scales.
Plots the five calculated points correctly.
Draws a straight best-fit line that does not pass through the origin.
commonErrors: forces the line through the origin
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A straight line with a positive intercept near 0.03 s²·m.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Pivot distance d (m) 0.05, Period T (s) 0.92; Pivot distance d (m) 0.10, Period T (s) 0.85; Pivot distance d (m) 0.15, Period T (s) 0.91; Pivot distance d (m) 0.20, Period T (s) 0.98; Pivot distance d (m) 0.25, Period T (s) 1.07

parts.label: D
parts.text: Using your best-fit line, calculate an experimental value for \(I_{cm}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses the vertical intercept of the best-fit line, consistent with part B.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Uses \(T^2d\) of the first row as the intercept.

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \(I_{cm}\) between about \(0.0030\) and \(0.0050\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

sampleResponse: A Hang the bar from five different holes, measure each \(d\) from the pivot to the center of mass, displace it about 5°, and time 20 oscillations; divide by 20 and repeat three times per hole. B \(T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2(I_{cm} + md^2)}{mgd}\), so \(T^2d = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}d^2 + \dfrac{4\pi^2I_{cm}}{mg}\). The intercept is \(\dfrac{4\pi^2I_{cm}}{mg}\). C \(d^2\): 0.0025, 0.010, 0.0225, 0.040, 0.0625 m²; \(T^2d\): 0.042, 0.072, 0.124, 0.192, 0.286 s²·m; a straight best-fit line with slope near 4.0 and intercept near 0.032. D \(I_{cm} = \dfrac{0.032 \times 0.50 \times 9.8}{4\pi^2} \approx 0.0040\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

title: Pulling In the Dumbbells
topic: Qualitative/Quantitative Translation · Conservation of angular momentum

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Physics C: Mechanics Question 4 (Qualitative/Quantitative Translation)

stimulus.content: Figure 1 (overhead view): Overhead view of a student on a rotating stool, first with arms outstretched holding dumbbells, then with the dumbbells pulled in

prompt: A student sits on a stool that rotates on a frictionless vertical axle, holding a dumbbell in each outstretched hand. The rotational inertia of the student-stool-dumbbell system about the axle is \(I_i\), and the system rotates with angular speed \(\omega_i\). The student then pulls the dumbbells in close to the body, so the rotational inertia becomes \(I_f\), where \(I_f < I_i\).

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 160" width="360" height="160" role="img" aria-label="Overhead view of a student on a rotating stool, first with arms outstretched holding dumbbells, then with the dumbbells pulled in" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="90" cy="80" r="18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><line x1="20" y1="80" x2="160" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="20" cy="80" r="8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="160" cy="80" r="8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><text x="90" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Initial: Iᵢ, ωᵢ</text><circle cx="270" cy="80" r="18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><line x1="238" y1="80" x2="302" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="238" cy="80" r="8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="302" cy="80" r="8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor"/><text x="270" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Final: I_f, ω_f</text><path d="M60 40 A40 40 0 0 1 120 40" stroke="#ec4899" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M245 50 A30 30 0 0 1 295 50" stroke="#ec4899" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
figures.alt: Overhead view of a student on a rotating stool, first with arms outstretched holding dumbbells, then with the dumbbells pulled in
figures.caption: Figure 1 (overhead view)

parts.label: A
parts.text: Indicate whether the rotational kinetic energy of the system increases, decreases, or remains the same as the student pulls in the dumbbells. Justify your answer using qualitative reasoning beyond referencing equations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that the rotational kinetic energy increases.
commonErrors: indicates it stays the same because angular momentum is conserved

rubricPoints.criterion: States that angular momentum is conserved because there is no net external torque about the axle, so the smaller rotational inertia requires a larger angular speed.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: No external torque acts, so as the mass moves inward the system must spin faster to keep the same angular momentum.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the source of the added energy: the student does positive work pulling the dumbbells inward (converting internal chemical energy).
commonErrors: claims energy is conserved for the system
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The student’s arms do work pulling the dumbbells inward against their tendency to move outward.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Derive an expression for the ratio \(\dfrac{K_f}{K_i}\) of the final to initial rotational kinetic energy in terms of \(I_i\) and \(I_f\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes conservation of angular momentum, \(I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f\).
Uses \(K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\) (or \(K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}\)) for both states.
Arrives at \(\dfrac{K_f}{K_i} = \dfrac{I_i}{I_f}\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: Indicate whether your expression from part B is or is not consistent with your answer to part A. Justify by referencing the expression.

rubricPoints.criterion: References the expression: since \(I_f < I_i\), the ratio \(I_i/I_f\) is greater than 1.
commonErrors: restates part A without the expression

rubricPoints.criterion: Correctly concludes the kinetic energy increases, consistent with part A (or identifies an inconsistency with an incorrect part A).
commonErrors: claims consistency with a contradicting part A
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: So K_f > K_i, which is consistent with part A.

sampleResponse: A It increases. No external torque acts about the axle, so the system's angular momentum is constant; pulling the dumbbells inward lowers the rotational inertia, so the system spins faster. The extra kinetic energy comes from the work the student's arms do pulling the dumbbells inward. B \(I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f = L\), and \(K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}\), so \(\dfrac{K_f}{K_i} = \dfrac{I_i}{I_f}\). C Consistent: \(I_f < I_i\), so the ratio exceeds 1 and \(K_f > K_i\).
